props.title: What a Way to Go!

sections.content: What a Way to Go! (1964) stands as one of Hollywood's most lavish dark comedies, starring Shirley MacLaine as Louisa May Foster, a woman whose husbands keep dying and leaving her increasingly wealthy. The film's outrageous production design and costume changes (over 70 costumes for MacLaine by Edith Head) rival The Young Girls of Rochefort (1967) and Funny Face (1957) in pure visual extravagance. Director J. Lee Thompson deliberately parodies different film genres with each husband's story, from silent comedy to European art films, creating a meta-commentary on 1960s cinema itself.

sections.content: The film's incredible cast reads like a who's who of 1960s leading men: Dick Van Dyke, Paul Newman, Robert Mitchum, Gene Kelly, and Dean Martin. Each brings their signature style to their doomed husband role, with Kelly particularly shining in a segment that parodies French New Wave cinema. This casting coup rivals other star-studded 1960s comedies like It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World (1963) and Casino Royale (1967).

The film's surreal production design by Jack Martin Smith and Ted Haworth creates distinct worlds for each husband, from a pink-saturated department store to a modernist art studio. This approach to segmented storytelling and varied visual styles influenced later anthology comedies like Amazon Women on the Moon (1987) and The Kentucky Fried Movie (1977). sections.content: Edith Head's costume design for What a Way to Go! represents the apex of 1960s Hollywood fashion excess, rivaling her work in Sweet Charity (1969) and Thoroughly Modern Millie (1967). MacLaine's wardrobe, which reportedly cost over $500,000 (equivalent to several million today), exemplifies the era's maximalist approach to costume design, setting a standard that influenced films like Valley of the Dolls (1967).
